title: Vectors
description: Components, magnitude, addition, the scalar product and the angle between two vectors

notes.heading: Vectors, Components and Magnitude
notes.body:
A **vector** has both magnitude and direction; a **scalar** has magnitude only. In two dimensions we write
$$\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$$
and in three dimensions $\mathbf{a} = (x, y, z) = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + z\mathbf{k}$.

The **magnitude** (length) comes from Pythagoras:
$$|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \qquad |\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$$

💡 **Worked Example** — For $\mathbf{a} = (3, 4)$: $|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$. For $\mathbf{b} = (2, -1, 2)$: $|\mathbf{b}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$.

📌 The vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is the position vector of $B$ minus the position vector of $A$: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$. Its magnitude is the distance $AB$.

notes.heading: Addition, Subtraction and Scalar Multiplication
notes.body:
Vectors combine component by component:
$$\begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 + b_1 \\ a_2 + b_2 \end{pmatrix} \qquad k\begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ka_1 \\ ka_2 \end{pmatrix}$$

Geometrically, $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$ is the diagonal of the parallelogram with sides $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ (the tip-to-tail rule), and $-\mathbf{a}$ points in the opposite direction with the same length.

💡 **Worked Example** — With $\mathbf{a} = (1, 2)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (2, -1)$:
$$3\mathbf{a} - 2\mathbf{b} = (3, 6) - (4, -2) = (-1, 8)$$
Check the magnitude: $|3\mathbf{a} - 2\mathbf{b}| = \sqrt{1 + 64} = \sqrt{65}$.

📌 Multiplication by a positive scalar $k$ multiplies the length by $k$ and leaves the direction unchanged; a negative $k$ reverses the direction.

notes.heading: The Scalar Product
notes.body:
The **scalar product** (dot product) of two vectors is a number, defined in two equivalent ways:
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}|\,|\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3$$
where $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors when placed tail to tail.

The component form is the one you use in calculations; the geometric form is the one you use to talk about angles.

💡 **Worked Example** — With $\mathbf{a} = (2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (-1, 3)$:
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = (2)(-1) + (1)(3) = -2 + 3 = 1$$
In three dimensions, $(1, 2, 2) \cdot (3, 0, -1) = 3 + 0 - 2 = 1$.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Multiplying the magnitudes by the components, or forgetting that the result is a scalar, not a vector.

notes.heading: The Angle Between Two Vectors
notes.body:
Rearranging the scalar product gives the angle formula, which is on the formula booklet:
$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|\,|\mathbf{b}|}$$

💡 **Worked Example** — Find the angle between $\mathbf{a} = (1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (1, 1)$.
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 1 \qquad |\mathbf{a}| = 1 \qquad |\mathbf{b}| = \sqrt2$$
$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{1 \times \sqrt2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \;\Longrightarrow\; \theta = 45^\circ$$

💡 **A three-dimensional case** — For $\mathbf{a} = (1, 2, 2)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (2, -1, 0)$: $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 2 - 2 + 0 = 0$, so the vectors are perpendicular and $\theta = 90^\circ$.

📌 The angle is always between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. If $\cos\theta$ comes out negative, the angle is obtuse — do not simply drop the sign.

notes.heading: Perpendicular and Parallel Vectors
notes.body:
Two facts cover almost every exam question about positions:

• $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are **perpendicular** exactly when $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0$.
• $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are **parallel** exactly when $\mathbf{a} = k\mathbf{b}$ for some scalar $k$.

💡 **Worked Example (perpendicularity)** — Find $p$ so that $\mathbf{a} = (2, 1, -1)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (1, p, 3)$ are perpendicular.
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 2 + p - 3 = p - 1 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; p = 1$$

💡 **Worked Example (parallelism)** — $(4, -6)$ and $(6, -9)$ are parallel because $(4, -6) = \dfrac{2}{3}(6, -9)$.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Testing parallelism with the dot product. A zero dot product means perpendicular, never parallel (only a zero vector is both, and that is a degenerate case).

notes.heading: Unit Vectors
notes.body:
A **unit vector** has magnitude 1. The unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{a}$ is
$$\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|}$$
Find the magnitude, then divide each component by it. The symbols $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{k}$ are the unit vectors along the coordinate axes.

💡 **Worked Example** — Find the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{a} = (1, 2, 2)$.
$$|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3 \;\Longrightarrow\; \hat{\mathbf{a}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$$
Check: $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1 + 4 + 4}{9} = 1$ ✓

📌 Every vector can be written as magnitude times a unit vector: $\mathbf{a} = |\mathbf{a}|\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}$. This is the standard way to answer "find a vector of length 10 in the direction of $\mathbf{a}$".

notes.heading: Vector Geometry and Exam Technique
notes.body:
Many geometry facts become one-line vector statements:

• **Midpoint** of $A$ and $B$: $\dfrac{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}}{2}$.
• **Distance** between two points: $|\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}|$.
• **Collinear** points: $\overrightarrow{AB} = k\,\overrightarrow{BC}$ for some scalar $k$.

💡 **Worked Example** — $A$ is $(1, 2, 3)$ and $B$ is $(5, -2, 1)$. Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and the position vector of the midpoint of $AB$.
$$\overrightarrow{AB} = (5 - 1, -2 - 2, 1 - 3) = (4, -4, -2)$$
$$\text{midpoint} = \dfrac{1}{2}\big[(1,2,3) + (5,-2,1)\big] = (3, 0, 2)$$
Also $AB = \sqrt{16 + 16 + 4} = 6$.

**Exam technique**
• Set out vectors in column or bracket notation with the components aligned; arithmetic slips dominate lost marks here.
• State the formula you are using before substituting, especially $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}$.
• If a question asks for an angle, give the answer in degrees or radians as requested, to the accuracy asked for.
• When a component is unknown, use the given condition — perpendicularity, parallelism or a stated magnitude — to build one equation.

questions.stem: Find the magnitude of the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$.
Which pair of vectors is perpendicular?
questions.explanation: Only $(2, 3) \cdot (3, -2) = 6 - 6 = 0$. The other pairs have non-zero scalar products, so they are not perpendicular.

questions.stem: Find the unit vector in the direction of $(0, 5)$.
questions.explanation: The magnitude is 5, so dividing gives $\left(\dfrac{0}{5}, \dfrac{5}{5}\right) = (0, 1)$, which has magnitude 1.

questions.stem: Find the angle between the vectors $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$.
Find the value of $k$ for which the vectors $(2, k)$ and $(3, -1)$ are perpendicular.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular means the scalar product is zero: $6 - k = 0$, so $k = 6$.

questions.stem: Find the unit vector in the direction of $(1, 2, 2)$.
questions.explanation: The magnitude is $\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$, so the unit vector is $\left(\dfrac13, \dfrac23, \dfrac23\right)$.

questions.stem: For $\mathbf{a} = (1, 2)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (3, -1)$, find $\cos\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between them.
Find the value of $p$ for which $(2, 1, -1)$ and $(1, p, 3)$ are perpendicular.
questions.explanation: The scalar product must be zero: $2(1) + 1(p) + (-1)(3) = p - 1 = 0$, so $p = 1$.

questions.stem: The vector $(3, k, 0)$ has magnitude 5. Find all possible values of $k$.
The points $A$ and $B$ have position vectors $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(5, -2, 1)$. Find the position vector of the midpoint of $AB$.

questions.explanation: $|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt5$, and multiplying a vector by 2 doubles its length, so $|2\mathbf{a}| = 2\sqrt5$.
